system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2151-11-19 01:30:00 to 2151-11-19 18:22:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of type 2 diabetes, kidney transplant, peripheral vascular disease, and prior amputations was admitted for osteomyelitis in the right index finger and right foot, presenting with pain, foul drainage, and fever. Imaging and biopsy confirmed bone infection in both sites. He underwent amputation of the right index finger tip and a transmetatarsal amputation of the right foot. Cultures grew Proteus mirabilis, sensitive to ertapenem. Due to equivocal margins in the foot, he was discharged on a prolonged course of outpatient IV ertapenem via a PICC line. His hypertension was managed with adjustment of labetalol to 600 mg twice daily, and his transplant function remained stable with continued immunosuppression. He was discharged home ambulatory with walker assistance, with plans for weekly lab monitoring and follow-up with podiatry and infectious disease.
problems: Diabetes with renal manifestations, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening, Mr. Johnson. I'm Dr. Patel, one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in because of some wounds on your foot that have been getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I’ve had three sores—one on my heel, one where my big toe used to be, and one on the side. The one on the side smells bad and has yellow drainage. It’s been painful too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned you’ve been on cefadroxil and doing daily dressing changes. Did your clinic suggest anything else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They did an incision and drainage, and wanted me to see Vascular Surgery, but I couldn’t get an appointment no matter how many times I called.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s frustrating. We’ve consulted Vascular Surgery here, and they recommend continuing medical management for now. We’re also concerned about infection, so we started you on IV antibiotics—vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and metronidazole—for broad coverage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need surgery? I’ve had so many procedures already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, the team doesn’t think surgery is needed. We did an X-ray of your foot, and while there’s swelling and skin thickening, we don’t see signs that the bone is infected—no osteomyelitis. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief. My blood pressure was really high when I came in—was that a concern?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was 251 over 122. I understand you didn’t take your blood pressure meds that day. We gave you labetalol and nifedipine in the ER, and now we’ve restarted your home medications. We also gave hydralazine once to help bring it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I usually take them, but I was feeling anxious about the foot and forgot. Is my kidney okay? I’ve had two transplants.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is 1.4, which is a bit higher than your usual 1.2, but it’s stable. We’re continuing your tacrolimus, prednisone, and leflunomide. The transplant team recommended admission to make sure everything stays on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes? My sugars have been high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping your insulin the same—Lantus at night and a sliding scale as needed. Your glucose was 284 when you arrived, but we’ll monitor it closely. Your A1c is high at 10.6%, so we’ll talk about long-term adjustments with your endocrinologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the antibiotics? How long will I be on them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching from IV to oral Bactrim—sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim—twice a day for seven days. It covers the likely bacteria, especially since pseudomonas is a concern with foot ulcers in patients with vascular disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my foot care at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Podiatry and Vascular Surgery recommend betadine dressings daily. You’ll need an outpatient ABI/PVR test to check blood flow in your leg. Depending on that, they may want an arteriogram. You’ll follow up with Dr. Lee in one week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that. And my blood pressure—I’ll make sure to take my meds every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your BP today is 129 over 74—much better. Just keep monitoring it at home. We’re discharging you today since you’re stable, comfortable, and able to manage your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad I can go home. I’ll keep up with the dressings and the antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Continue your other medications—pravastatin, aspirin, famotidine, and vitamins. Watch your blood sugar and BP, and call if the wound worsens or you develop fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my right finger. I had an amputation recently, and the stitches are still in. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The stitches should come out soon—follow up with your surgeon. As long as there’s no redness, swelling, or drainage, it’s likely healing fine. Keep it clean and dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better knowing what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll send the discharge instructions to your sister, and you’ll get a call from the follow-up team. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it. Have a good one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too, Mr. Johnson. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you’re cleared to leave. Nurse will bring your prescriptions and wound care supplies. Safe travels home.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of type 2 diabetes, kidney transplant, peripheral vascular disease, and prior amputations was admitted for worsening foot wounds on the right heel, lateral foot, and site of prior great toe amputation, with purulent drainage and foul odor. He had been unable to secure an outpatient vascular surgery appointment. Blood pressure was severely elevated on arrival, attributed to missed medications. Imaging showed soft tissue swelling without evidence of osteomyelitis. He was treated with IV antibiotics initially, then transitioned to oral Bactrim. Vascular and podiatry teams recommended medical management with betadine dressings and outpatient vascular studies. His hypertension improved with reinitiation of home medications, and transplant function remained stable. He was discharged home with follow-up plans and instructions for wound care and medication adherence.
